title: Favorite Lewis band musicians and the feel of time
summary: He admired Joe Watkins and Slow Drag's time and learned to swing naturally; Lawrence's strict ideas about who truly could play jazz.

story.theme_name: Drummers and drumming: who played what, and how
story.community_name: Great drummers: who they admired and why

blocks.x: Who did you like when you started playing? You mentioned Bonk, and then there must have been some other musicians. You said you met a lot on the mind.

Yeah, well, Bonk, and George, and Jim, and, uh, uh, let's see. I like the way Joe Watkins, was it Watkins who was playing with? I like the way Joe Watkins played time, you know. He wasn't much of a technician, but I kind of like the way he played time with the Lewis band. And of course drag had such a hell of a pulse, you know. The sitting back of drag, sitting in front of drag, you know, was really something. And, uh, and it really, really made me so, so conscious of this, this time thing, of just being able to lay back and have the time there. And that's, that's sort of grown up with me, you know, into modern jazz. And that's why so many guys think I played with such good time. And it's because of that background that I had. Uh, this, just feeling that, that, uh, you shouldn't worry about swinging, that you swing naturally. That the time will be there, you see. That the important thing is, is to express yourself and to do, uh, to create on your instrument, to not worry about swinging, that you'll swing naturally. And that, I think, is due to efforts of people like drag and Lawrence, and sitting with the Lewis band in the background. I did it.
Well, it's more or less that Lewis band that, that were your favorite out of that era.

Yeah, well, because there was nobody else to listen to, except on records. Uh, when I played with Barnes, there were very few times when his chops were up, you know, where he'd play something that was really meaningful. When he did, you know, it would really get to me. And, uh, it was really something to listen to. And so many of the other drummers would rush and, uh, retard or have some kind of problem here or there, you know. Same thing with the other instrumentalists. And then from what Lawrence was telling me, there were very few, very fine jazz musicians in the world. Right. And had been very few fine jazz musicians. He was very conscious of the ability to, uh, discern. He was, he was very, uh, particular in his likes and dislikes. And this got to me. He didn't feel that, that, uh, everybody could play jazz, and that everybody should be playing jazz, and that what everybody was playing should necessarily be called jazz because it prescribed the certain rules. He said that there was something that, that was objective, and he didn't say it in those words. But he implied that there was something objective in jazz that you could listen for. A genuineness and, and a sort of an artistic ability, I guess you could say, that was natural. And, uh, I think Bunk had it, uh, I think Jelly Roll had it. And, uh, I don't want to drop names because right now, you know, it's not a very easy thing to do anyway. Uh, but certainly a lot of people did have it, and a lot of people didn't have it, and it's been attributed to a lot of people who didn't have it. And Lawrence said that. And that's one of the things he was very strong about.
